results.summary_before: Simon's Caterpillar is a port of the Caterpillar Logic game to the Simon Says PMOD. The game has 20 levels where players deduce secret rules about color sequences. It uses a 7-segment display, LEDs, buttons, and a speaker for interaction. The design requires the Simon Says PMOD and runs at 50 kHz. Silicon testing by the author confirmed it works as expected.
results.summary: This project implements a simple serial 16-bit register (mini SPI) with magic cookie detection, plus a 16-bit delta-sigma modulator that can be configured for 1st or 2nd order. A LUT-based sine generator with programmable frequency can be selected to drive the modulator input. Testing involves serially loading the shift register, checking the magic cookie detection, inspecting the low and high output bytes, and monitoring the delta-sigma modulator's DC or sine output through an external RC low-pass filter. Only a way to set digital inputs is needed, with a scope or voltmeter useful for observing the outputs.

results.summary_before: This project is a 16-bit experimental CPU called GUS16 with a serial port, PWM output, general purpose I/O and an external memory interface, with memory provided off-chip. It includes a bootloader that loads programs over the serial port, and the documented basic test is to connect at 115200 baud, 8N1, and send an 'L', which should be echoed back. More complete testing requires an external board with SRAM and address latches attached to the user PMOD connectors, and that memory board is noted as still pending design. The design is documented in an accompanying PDF and occupies a 1x2 tile area.
results.summary: This project is a 4-bit multiplier that takes two 4-bit integers, m and q, and outputs their 8-bit product p. It was created using a manual structural design in which AND gates form the partial products and 1-bit full adders sum them while handling carries. The partial products are aligned diagonally to mimic manual binary multiplication. Testing is done by editing test.py in the test folder to add custom test cases, and no external hardware is required.

results.summary_before: Flame demo displays a flame animation on a VGA monitor and plays simple 1-bit PWM audio. It requires a TinyVGA PMOD for video and either Mike's audio PMOD or a basic RC filter for sound, and it runs at a 25 MHz clock with a reset pulse. Silicon testing by two independent testers confirmed that both audio and video work as expected, with good use of color and dithering. The design is a compact demoscene-style demo suitable for the Tiny Tapeout demo competition.
